definition: A cross-linked aromatic polymer in plant cell walls that stiffens and waterproofs tissue; in bast fibers it helps bind cells together and affects stiffness, color and processing.
explanation: Lignin fills spaces in secondary cell walls between cellulose microfibrils and hemicellulose, making woody tissue rigid, water resistant and harder for microbes to break down. It forms by oxidative coupling of monolignol radicals, so unlike cellulose or proteins it has no regular repeating sequence. Wood is heavily lignified, whereas textile bast fibers such as flax contain only a few percent, found partly in the outer secondary wall layer. Retting, scutching and chemical degumming aim to free fibers from the woody core and reduce the non-cellulosic material, including lignin, that would otherwise make yarn coarse and stiff.
example: A researcher compares two batches of hemp from the same field, one well retted and one under-retted. The under-retted batch feels stiffer and splits only into coarse strands, and chemical analysis shows more residual lignin and pectin holding its fiber bundles together. The comparison shows that processing, not just plant species, determines how much lignin reaches the yarn and how finely the fiber can be divided.
caution: Lignin is not cellulose and is not a textile fiber on its own. A reported lignin content depends on the analytical method, such as acid-insoluble residue, and on whether whole stems or isolated fibers were analyzed, so figures from different studies may not be comparable. Research into lignin-derived materials or low-lignin crops says nothing about what is in a particular commercial fabric.
deeper: Lignin is assembled from three monolignols, p-coumaryl, coniferyl and sinapyl alcohols, which enter the polymer as p-hydroxyphenyl (H), guaiacyl (G) and syringyl (S) units. They differ in the number of methoxy groups on the aromatic ring, which affects how they can couple. Oxidized monolignol radicals join in several bond types, giving a heterogeneous network, and plants also incorporate minor phenylpropanoid units such as hydroxycinnamyl aldehydes and p-coumarates. In flax fiber, reported compositions are about 2 to 5% lignin alongside roughly 64 to 78% cellulose and 12 to 17% hemicellulose. In jute, transgenic suppression of monolignol biosynthesis genes lowered fiber lignin by about 13 to 14% relative to controls, showing that the pathway can be targeted to ease fiber processing.
origins: The name is built on the Latin lignum, wood. Once Payen had isolated cellulose from plant tissue in 1838, chemists turned to the other substances that held woody tissue together, and lignin became defined largely as what must be removed to obtain clean cellulose. Chemical pulping for paper and dissolving pulp still works mainly by stripping it out. Its exact structure proved hard to pin down because it forms by radical coupling rather than by a templated process.

definition: The central cavity inside a plant fiber cell, left as the cell wall thickens; its size and collapse shape cotton's twisted form and relate directly to fiber maturity.
explanation: Plant fibers are single cells, or bundles of cells, whose walls thicken from the outside inward. A cotton fiber begins as a tubular seed hair with a wide central cavity, and as the secondary wall deposits cellulose, that cavity narrows. When the boll opens and the fiber dries, the cell collapses into a flattened, bean-shaped cross-section with a small residual lumen, and this collapse contributes to the characteristic twists along the fiber. Bast fibers such as flax also have a central lumen, surrounded by thick secondary walls built in layers. Because the lumen is an internal space, it can hold water and treatment chemicals.
example: Students cut cross-sections of immature and mature cotton fibers and view them under a microscope. The immature fibers show thin walls around a large, flattened lumen and look ribbon-like, while the mature fibers have thick walls and only a small central cavity. The class then relates what they see to the circularity and wall-thickening ratios that laboratories use to express cotton maturity numerically.
caution: A plant fiber's lumen is a natural cell cavity, not the engineered hollow core of some manufactured fibers. Lumen size alone does not measure maturity, which depends on wall thickness relative to the fiber's perimeter. Animal fibers do not have a lumen: the core some of them contain is the medulla, a different structure made of cells and air spaces.
deeper: In a growing cotton fiber the lumen occupies roughly a third of the cross-section, and after drying and collapse it shrinks to about 5% or less. Maturity is expressed through measurements on cross-sections: circularity C equals 4 pi A divided by the square of the perimeter, and the degree of thickening Tr equals 2 pi T divided by the perimeter, where A is the wall area and T the wall thickness; both range from 0 to 1. In flax, each elementary fiber has a lumen enclosed by a primary wall and a secondary wall in three sublayers, S1 next to the primary wall, then S2, and S3 lining the lumen. In the living plant the lumen carries water and nutrients by capillary action.
origins: Lumen is Latin for light, and by extension an opening, and anatomists use it for the cavity of any tube, from blood vessels to plant cells. In fiber science it names the space left inside a cell once its wall has formed. Cotton breeders and testers have long linked lumen and wall development to maturity, and cross-sectional image analysis in the late twentieth century was used to develop reference standards for cotton maturity measurement.
